title: The future seen from the past

sections.title: Expressing the future from the past
sections.content:
There are a number of ways of talking about an activity or event that was in the future at a particular point in the past. In order to express this idea, we can use the past tenses of the verb forms we would normally use to talk about the future. These forms are often used in reporting (see Units 32–36).
Compare the following sentences:
Future from now: I haven't got much money, so I think I'll stay at home this summer.
Future from the past: Eleni decided that she would stay at home for the summer.
Future from now: I'm not going to say anything about the exams today, because I don't have time.
Future from the past: I wasn't going to say anything about the exams, but the students asked me to.
Future from now: I'm having a meeting with my tutor tomorrow to discuss my work.
Future from the past: I couldn't go to the match because I was having a meeting with my tutor.
Future from now: Will you be going alone, or is Louise going with you?
Future from the past: At the time, I thought I would be going alone, but then Jan said he wanted to come.
Future from now: The exam will have finished by three o'clock, so I'll see you then.
Future from the past: The exam was so easy that most people would have finished after 30 minutes.
Future from now: There is to be a meeting of ministers this evening.
Future from the past: It was announced that there was to be a meeting of ministers that evening.
Future from now: When the school closes, all the children are to be moved to one nearby.
Future from the past: Mrs Novak heard that she was to be moved to a post in a nearby school.
Future from now: As the bell is about to go for the end of the lesson, pack your books away.
Future from the past: The bell was about to go when all the children started to pack their books away.
If the future seen from the past is still in the future for the speaker, then either form is possible:
• It was announced this morning that there is / was to be a statement this evening.
In some cases, we don't know whether the activity or event happened or not. Compare:
• I didn't phone to give him the news because we were seeing each other later. He was very upset when I told him. (= we saw each other)
• We were seeing each other later that day, but I had to phone and cancel. (= we didn't see each other)

sections.title: Was/were to + infinitive; was/were to have + past participle
sections.content:
To talk about an activity or event that was in the future at a particular point in the past, we can use was / were to + infinitive (for things that actually happened) and was / were to have + past participle (for things that were expected, but didn't happen):
• At the time she was probably the best actor in the theatre company, but in fact some of her colleagues were to become much better known.
• The boat, which was to have taken them to the island, failed to arrive.
• He was to find out years later that the car he had bought was stolen.
Note, however, that in less formal contexts it is more natural to use be supposed to:
• I was supposed to help, but I was ill. (more natural than I was to have helped …)

exercises.question: I'm going to do the washing, but we'd run out of washing powder.
options: was going to do ✓ (future from past)
exercises.hint: Past point of view: 'I had plans to...' → was going to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was going to do ✓ (future from past)
Was going to expresses a future intention or plan seen from a past viewpoint — often one that did not happen or was abandoned. It is the past equivalent of be going to for expressing prior plans and future-from-past expectations.

exercises.question: The concert tonight would be over by about 9:30. We could eat after that.
exercises.hint: 'Would be over' is correct — future from past perspective.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Correct ✓ (future from past with 'would')
We use would here for past habits, hypothetical situations, or reported speech.
💡 'Would be over' is correct — future from past perspective.

exercises.question: When we were passing Ivan's house, we thought we'd drop in and see him.
options: Correct ✓ (past continuous for future from past)
exercises.hint: Past continuous ('were passing') for planned/ongoing future from past — correct.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Correct ✓ (past continuous for future from past)
Past continuous ('were passing') for planned/ongoing future from past — correct.

exercises.question: A: Sorry, I thought Ella will have shown you. Over there.
options: would have shown ✓ (future perfect from past)
exercises.hint: Future perfect from past → would have shown.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: would have shown ✓ (future perfect from past)
We use would here for past habits, hypothetical situations, or reported speech.
💡 Future perfect from past → would have shown.

exercises.question: He said he ___ (call) me the next morning, but he never did.
exercises.hint: Future-in-the-past, reported intention → would or was going to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: would call
'Would' is the past form of 'will' and is used in reported speech to express a future event seen from a past perspective. 'Was going to' also works, emphasising the intention.

exercises.question: The manager of Newtown United said that the team is to be announced at nine tomorrow.
exercises.hint: Still in future for speaker → both 'is to be' and 'was to be' are possible.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Both are possible
Still in future for speaker → both 'is to be' and 'was to be' are possible.

exercises.question: The second half was about to start, so we had to go back to our seats now.
options: Correct ✓ (was about to = imminent future from past)
exercises.hint: 'Was about to start' = correct future from past (very imminent).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Correct ✓ (was about to = imminent future from past)
'Was about to start' = correct future from past (very imminent).

exercises.question: I knew that by the morning I would be feeling exhausted, but I just wanted to go dancing.
options: Correct ✓ (future continuous from past = 'would be feeling')
exercises.hint: 'Would be feeling' = future continuous from past — correct.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Correct ✓ (future continuous from past = 'would be feeling')
We use would here for past habits, hypothetical situations, or reported speech.
💡 'Would be feeling' = future continuous from past — correct.

exercises.question: B: He is supposed to be here yesterday, and there's still no sign of him.
options: was supposed to be here ✓ (past → was supposed to)
had been supposed to be here
exercises.hint: Yesterday → past tense: 'was supposed to be'.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was supposed to be here ✓ (past → was supposed to)
Yesterday → past tense: 'was supposed to be'.

exercises.question: I had a feeling the interview ___ (not / go) well. I was right.
exercises.hint: Prediction/sense about the future from a past viewpoint → was going to.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: was not going to go
'Was going to' expresses a prediction or expectation about the future as seen from the past. It is also used for intentions that were planned but not fulfilled.

exercises.question: I'm about to ask the same question.
exercises.hint: 'I'm about to ask' = imminent future from now — correct.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Correct ✓ (present = about to ask)
'I'm about to ask' = imminent future from now — correct.

exercises.question: DNA testing was to be used by police in the search for the missing Dublin schoolboy.
options: Correct ✓ (formal future-from-past: was to be used)
exercises.hint: 'Was to be used' = formal future from past in news context — correct.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Correct ✓ (formal future-from-past: was to be used)
'Was to be used' = formal future from past in news context — correct.

exercises.question: We are meeting at seven in the Globe coffee bar. Can you be there, too?
exercises.hint: Still future for speaker → present continuous 'are meeting' is correct.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: Correct ✓ (present continuous for future arrangement)
Still future for speaker → present continuous 'are meeting' is correct.

exercises.question: We didn't expect that having a rabbit as a pet will cause so many problems.
options: would cause ✓ (future from past in a 'that' clause)
exercises.hint: Inside a past-tense reporting verb → would cause (not will cause).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: would cause ✓ (future from past in a 'that' clause)
We use would here for past habits, hypothetical situations, or reported speech.
💡 Inside a past-tense reporting verb → would cause (not will cause).

exercises.question: Little did she know that those ___ (be) the last words he ever spoke to her.
exercises.hint: Formal/literary future seen from past → were to be.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: were to be
'Be to' in the past tense expresses events that were destined to happen or that became clear in retrospect. It is common in literary and narrative writing to describe significance seen from hindsight.

exercises.question: The meeting was to have taken place in the hall, but ___
options: a: had to be cancelled at the last minute. (= didn't happen)
b: and was well attended. (= happened)
a: had to be cancelled at the last minute. (= doesn't happen)
a: had to be cancelled at the last minute. (= didn't happen)ing
exercises.hint: 'Was to have taken' = expected but didn't happen → it was cancelled.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: a: had to be cancelled at the last minute. (= didn't happen)
'Was to have taken' = expected but didn't happen → it was cancelled. 'Was to have taken' = expected but didn't happen → it was cancelled — look for the context signals in the sentence that point to this specific grammatical form.

exercises.question: She was to have appeared with the actor in his last film…
options: b: but the part went to her sister. (= didn't happen)
a: and was a tremendous success. (= happened)
b: but the part went to her sister. (= doesn't happen)
b: but the part went to her sister. (= didn't happen)ing
exercises.hint: 'Was to have appeared' = expected but didn't → part went to sister.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: b: but the part went to her sister. (= didn't happen)
'Was to have appeared' = expected but didn't → part went to sister. 'Was to have appeared' = expected but didn't → part went to sister — look for the context signals in the sentence that point to this specific grammatical form.

exercises.question: Later, in Rome, I was to meet Professor Pearce …
options: b: and was very impressed by his knowledge of Italian culture. (= happened)
a: but he left before I got there. (= didn't happen)
a: but he left before I got there. (= doesn't happen)
b: and had been very impressed by his knowledge of Italian culture. (= happened)
exercises.hint: 'Was to meet' (without have) = it actually happened.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: b: and was very impressed by his knowledge of Italian culture. (= happened)
'Was to meet' (without have) = it actually happened. The grammatical signals in this sentence — the key words, connectors, or context — require this specific form. Look for these signals to make the same choice independently.

exercises.question: It was to take 48 hours to get to Japan …
options: b: but we managed to do it in only a day. (= didn't happen as expected)
a: and we were exhausted when we arrived.
b: but we managed to do it in only a day. (= doesn't happen as expected)
b: but we managed to do it in only a day. (= didn't happen as expected)ing
exercises.hint: 'Was to take' describes expected duration; 'but' = it actually took less.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: b: but we managed to do it in only a day. (= didn't happen as expected)
'Was to take' describes expected duration; 'but' = it actually took less. The present simple is correct here. Check the context: is this a permanent fact, a habitual action, a performative declaration, or a stative verb describing a state? All of these take the present simple rather than the continuous.

exercises.question: The bridge was to have been completed this year …
options: a: but a number of accidents have led to delays. (= wasn't completed)
b: and is to be opened by the president next month.
a: but a number of accidents have led to delays. (= wasn't completed)ing
b: and is to be opened by the president next month.ing
exercises.hint: 'Was to have been completed' = planned but not done → delays.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: a: but a number of accidents have led to delays. (= wasn't completed)
'Was to have been completed' = planned but not done → delays. The present perfect links past events to the present. The key signals are: just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for, recently, and incomplete time expressions like this week or today (when not yet over).
